1.3a — Your First Script: Variables & Update

Today you write C# that runs inside your game. Not the player's code — that already works. Your own tiny script, from scratch, so the big one stops being magic.

Predict First ~10 min

Open Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs and look at the skeleton that runs on the Player right now:

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    private Animator anim;

    private void Start()
    {
        anim = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>();
        if (anim != null)
        {
            anim.SetBool("IsWalking", true);
        }
    }
}

Notice what is here — and what is missing. There is a Start() method that grabs the Animator and starts the walk cycle, but there is no Update() method yet! Predict before running anything: if you add an Update() method with Debug.Log("hello") inside it, roughly how many times does "hello" print in ten seconds? Ten? One? Something much bigger? Write your answer down — we check it after you build your own script.

Socratic

The class name is PlayerController and the file is PlayerController.cs. Why does Unity force that match, when a regular program would happily let you rename a file?

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — create the script. In the Project window, right-click Assets/Scripts → Create → C# Script (or, in newer Unity: Create → Scripting → MonoBehaviour Script). Name it PlayerLogger — the file must match the class exactly. Open it. Unity writes you a starter that gives you two methods: Start and Update.

Step 2 — add a field. Inside the class, above the methods:

[SerializeField] private float reportDelay = 1.0f;
private float nextReportTime = 0f;

A normal private field is the script's secret. But prefixing it with [SerializeField] instructs Unity to expose it as an editable knob in the Inspector window without making it accessible to other scripts.

Step 3 — print on a timer. In Update:

private void Update()
{
    if (Time.time >= nextReportTime)
    {
        Debug.Log("Still here at " + Time.time);
        nextReportTime = nextReportTime + reportDelay;
    }
}

Step 4 — attach it. Drag PlayerLogger.cs onto the Player in the Hierarchy (or Add Component → Player Logger). Scripts are components — attaching is how a GameObject gets the ability. Press Play and read the Console.

Bug Hunt: Break the logger on purpose

Make each bug, run it, explain the Console, then fix it:

  1. Rename the class playerLogger (lowercase p) in the code only. What does Unity say when you press Play?
  2. Drag the script onto the Turret instead of the Player and play. Does it still print — and what does that tell you about which object a script belongs to?
  3. Change the condition to if (Time.time > nextReportTime + reportDelay). What changed about the rhythm, and can you explain why?
  4. Delete the whole nextReportTime update line. What fills the Console, and why is that a problem for your first answer in the Predict block?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Make the logger useful

  1. Make it print the player's position instead of the time — Google is allowed: search "unity transform.position". What kind of value does transform.position hold?
  2. Change reportDelay to 0.25 in the Inspector while playing. Does the change survive after you press stop, and why?
  3. Give the logger a second [SerializeField] int called maxReports and stop logging after that many. Where did you put the check — and would a while loop have worked here instead?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Create a new C# script and attach it to a GameObject
  • Explain what runs, when: Start once vs Update every frame
  • Write a [SerializeField] private field and tune it in the Inspector
  • Explain the difference between a class name and a file name
  • Use Debug.Log + a timer instead of spamming every frame
